title: The manjis, deeper
hook: his network of teachers, women and men, spread the sangat far

segments.voice: Yesterday, dying in the Word: ego's grip breaking, so that real living can start. Your line was die to ego. Which clever reply did you let go? Day one thousand one hundred eighty-eight.

A low wooden frame, rope woven across it, a household cot or seat of the kind used in Punjabi courtyards. Nothing grand. Sit on it under a tree and people can gather on the ground around you. Sikh tradition says that's the picture behind a word from Guru Amar Das's time: manji. He lived at Goindval, and the sangat kept growing in places far from his door. So, tradition says, he appointed teachers, women and men, to sit on a manji in their own region and hold the sangat together there.
screen: `A SMALL ROPE SEAT.` → `PEOPLE GATHER AROUND IT.` → `TEACHERS, WOMEN AND MEN.`

segments.voice: We've met the manjis before on this path, as a story. Today let's look at what kind of idea they were. First, a manji was a plain household seat, not a throne. The teacher sat close to the people, near enough to hear their questions. The authority came from the Guru's teaching, not from the furniture. Second, it moved the center outward. Instead of everyone having to travel to one place, the sangat could meet near home. The Guru's Word, the langar's open row, the hymns: all of it could happen in a village courtyard. Third, tradition remembers women among these teachers. The Guru's network trusted them to lead. Accounts differ on the details. The heart of the telling is that the sangat spread far. And what was a manji meant to hold? Guru Nanak had already given the measure, in Sri Rag. Paraphrased: how is the true sangat known? Where the One Name is spoken. That's the test of a manji. Not the size of the crowd, not the fame of the teacher. Whether the Name is spoken there. Here's the part that reaches an ordinary week. A Sikh who explains a hymn to a child, or invites a coworker to langar, is doing in a small way what the manjis did: carrying the sangat a little further from the center, and sitting close enough to listen.
screen: `A SEAT, NOT A THRONE.` · `THE CENTER MOVES OUTWARD.` · `WOMEN TRUSTED TO LEAD.` · `WHERE THE ONE NAME IS SPOKEN.` · then, large: `SPREAD IT FAR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: teach one person. In the sit, let the breath slow, and let one thing you've learned on this path come back to you. Man too jot saroop hai. By any door. Not the pyre. Choose the one you understand well enough to say simply. Then think of one person who might like to hear it: a child, a friend, a parent. Picture yourself sitting beside them, saying it in your own plain words, and listening to what they ask. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
The manjis. In Sikh tradition, the seats of teachers, women and men, who held the sangat together far from the Guru's town, wherever the Name was spoken. Today's word.
Your line: spread it far. Today, tell the one person the one thing you chose, simply, and leave room for their question. Day one thousand one hundred eighty-eight.

howItsDone: Sikhs remember the manji system in histories of Guru Amar Das and in katha; today local gurdwaras and their sangats carry on the work of gathering people near home around the Guru's Word.
